video_title: The Evolution of the Russian Military - Its Strengths and Shortfalls in 2026 (With Michael Kofman)
gist: Perun interviews Michael Kofman on how the Russian military's flawed 2022 force design (under-manned, mobilization-dependent, hedge-free) gave way to a larger contract-recruited force that can no longer grow and fights via small infiltrations, while improving sharply in drone-enabled reconnaissance-strike. Part one of two; argues Russia is stronger in mass and fires but weaker in large-scale maneuver, and that Ukrainian adaptation explains slower 2026 advances.

insights.claim: Russia entered 2022 with a force designed around precision strike, indirect fire and aerospace assault, assuming prolonged positional wars were 20th-century relics, so it cut infantry and logistics and left no hedge if those bets were wrong.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Force-design bets without hedges fail catastrophically when the war differs from the assumed one.
insights.quote: they had assumed that prolonged positional traditional fights were long over and that these were the wars of the 20th century

insights.claim: The pre-2022 Russian military relied on a dual-generation model (contract battalion tactical groups plus conscripts) that presumed partial mobilization for any large war, so the peacetime force was kept cheaply under-manned.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: The model was cheap but depended on a political decision that was not made in time.

insights.claim: Russia expanded force structure on paper from brigades toward divisions without growing total personnel, so manning fell; a mechanized company nominally of about 100 men shrank to about 76 authorized and roughly 59-60 actually present, leaving very few dismounts.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Under-resourced paper expansion produced the infantry shortage seen in the invasion.

insights.claim: Only about 40% of overall Russian ground force capacity was generated for the initial invasion, because the army depended on a mobilization that Putin did not order until September 2022 after the defeat at Kharkiv; roughly seven months of manpower bleed followed.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Military planning assumptions collided with political unwillingness to pay the cost of mobilizing.

insights.claim: Perun argues a cheap war is often the most expensive: Russia's under-resourced invasion lost equipment that lacked infantry screening, lost stockpile positions, and took heavy casualties among hard-to-replace pre-war contract troops and junior officers.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: False economies in the opening phase created costs that lasted years.

insights.claim: Other militaries should wargame how a plan could go wrong and avoid militarily convenient assumptions that ignore political reality, since such disconnects can be papered over in peacetime but prove catastrophic in war.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Applicable as a stress test for any force design or corporate plan resting on a convenient assumption.

insights.claim: Russia's wartime expansion rested on contract recruitment through payouts rather than classical mobilization: over 1.3 million contracted, and the September 2022 mobilized personnel represent perhaps 15% or less of all personnel used in the war.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Russia sustained a large war without repeated mobilization, unlike smaller Ukraine.

insights.claim: Mobilized personnel in autumn 2022 were split into about 170,000 for roughly 70 new reserve regiments equipped from Soviet storage and about 100,000 to fill out forces in Ukraine; active-duty strength grew from about 850,000 pre-invasion to 1.3-1.4 million, with over 700,000 deployed in and around Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Gives scale of the expansion and the role of Soviet stockpiles.

insights.claim: Russia recruited over 400,000 in each of 2024 and 2025 and has a 2026 quota of 409,000 (about 33-35,000 per month), but since summer 2025 irreplaceable losses (killed and seriously wounded) have matched or exceeded monthly recruitment.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Recruitment now only replaces losses, so net force growth has stalled.
insights.quote: irreplaceable losses, those killed and seriously wounded have not only matched but in many months exceeded the monthly recruitment totals

insights.claim: Putin's stated troop numbers in the war zone rose to about 617,000 in late 2023 and plateaued at about 700,000 through 2024 and late 2025, and the authorized strength rose only about 47,000 by October against a 400,000-plus recruitment target; this suggests recruitment no longer enlarges the force.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The expansion phase appears to have hit diminishing returns around 2025.

insights.claim: Russia assumed in 2023-24 that growing mass and material from industry (about 15%) and Soviet storage would grind Ukraine down, but the larger the force grew the less of it could be employed at tactical level, with offensive action now mostly one-to-two-man infiltrations and small fire teams.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Mass without employment capacity does not convert to breakthroughs.
insights.quote: The larger the Russian force grew in Ukraine in terms of force density and overall forces deployed, the less of it they were able to employ at the tactical level.

insights.claim: Russia has lost about 24,000 pieces of equipment yet likely has more tanks in the force than at the start of the war, so quantity is not its problem; force employment is.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Equipment-loss tallies understate Russian material capacity.

insights.claim: Ukrainian shifts of manpower into drone units plus mining and artillery made mechanized assaults and any force concentration non-viable, and mine-artillery-drone combinations counter any assault configuration, so tactics shrank from battalion tactical groups down to fire teams.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Defensive drone-mine systems neutralise Russia's quantitative edge.

insights.claim: Russian contract recruits get two weeks of training or less and are thrown into units without cohesion, and junior and mid-level leaders lost early in the war take years to rebuild, so large-scale combined arms offensives are currently out of reach.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Russia cannot exploit a localized Ukrainian collapse at operational scale, and its options against NATO would be limited.

insights.claim: Russia runs persistent offensives from late February/March through November/December rather than discrete seasonal offensives, driven by political pressure to show results, which prevents the force from restoring offensive potential.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Continuous pressure trades long-term capability for short-term pressure.

insights.claim: The attritional grind reflects Russian military culture as an artillery army (Soviet and Imperial before), whose doctrine seeks a decisive fires advantage; doctrine written for a NATO war (maneuver defense, then counterattack) did not fit Ukraine, and the army reverted to its destruction-oriented model.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: The grinding style is not the planned Russian way of war but a reversion to organizational type.

insights.claim: Kofman argues a force optimized for the highest-intensity scenario (such as China-US over Taiwan) is wrongly assumed to handle all lesser contingencies, since different war types need substantial adaptation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Planning to the worst case does not cover the lesser-included cases.

insights.claim: Russia has become better at reconnaissance-fire and reconnaissance-strike, combining ISR drones, a real-time data layer and fire control with strike assets, fixing the historical Soviet problem of firepower with blindness; the threat zone near the front now deters vehicle movement.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: The most dangerous Russian improvement is in its traditional strength, fires.

insights.claim: Russia has built drone platoons in motorized battalions, drone companies and battalions at higher echelons, elite independent drone units such as Rubicon, independent drone regiments and brigades, plus a UGV component and its own unmanned systems force, reallocating manpower structurally.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: These are genuine force-structure changes rather than fleeting adaptations.

insights.claim: Robin Dema argues Russia's drone organization, with strike assets integrated under division commanders, is better to copy than Ukraine's more independent USF model, where army corps can only ask and not order the drone forces.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Countries with time to build capability may prefer integrated command over Ukraine's quickly improvised structure.

insights.claim: A Russian commander now has Garan drones ranging 1,000 km, ISR swarms, loitering munitions, FPVs, bomber drones and UGVs, plus jet-powered one-way attack drones and mini cruise missiles, which likely eclipses typical NATO units in quantity and experience.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: NATO units lag in drone quantity and experience.

insights.claim: Drone operators and fires coordinators face lower casualty churn than assault infantry, so Russia's drone and fires experience has accumulated while assault infantry experience stays rare.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Capability is concentrating in enablers not infantry.

insights.claim: Kofman says it is not possible to separate force quality from battlefield conditions; a Western force would face the same drone-mine defense and would not simply breeze through, and Western militaries with little large-scale training should not assume it would be easy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Warns against complacency in NATO that these tactics reflect Russian incompetence.
insights.quote: People are not fighting this way in this war just because it hadn't occurred to them that they could do it much differently.

insights.claim: Air power is no magic spell: even localized air superiority does not automatically solve breaching prepared defenses or mass precision on the battlefield.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Counters the belief that air superiority removes the Ukrainian-style defensive problem.

insights.claim: Perun judges that a 2026 Russian military dropped into February 2022 would likely have done worse for Ukraine, while the 2026 Ukrainian defenders would probably have beaten back the 2022 invasion; Russia is weaker in maneuver, troop quality, interceptors, munitions stocks, the Black Sea Fleet and strategic bombers, yet stronger in mass, drones and fires.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russia's maneuver may have atrophied, but its shooting capability and mass have grown.
insights.quote: this is a historically shooty military that in some ways has become even more shooty

insights.claim: Slower Russian advances in 2026 are explained less by Russian decline than by Ukrainian combined technological, tactical and organizational adaptation, so Ukraine deserves credit and its methods should be studied.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Territory gained is a poor proxy for Russian military capability trend.
